cls: Urinary tract analgesic / bladder protectant (semisynthetic sulfated polysaccharide)
pharm: Semisynthetic, heparin-like sulfated polysaccharide with weak anticoagulant and fibrinolytic activity that is thought to adhere to the bladder urothelium and restore the protective glycosaminoglycan layer, relieving interstitial cystitis pain.
quick: 100 mg by mouth three times daily (300 mg/day) on an empty stomach
Take on an empty stomach - 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals
Limited data; use only if clearly needed (heparin-like; bleeding considerations)
No specific adjustment established; use caution
Use with caution in hepatic impairment (anticoagulant component)
Vision/retina (pigmentary maculopathy), signs of bleeding, liver function
summary: Pentosan polysulfate sodium is an orally administered, semisynthetic, sulfated polysaccharide (heparin-like) used for the relief of bladder pain or discomfort associated with interstitial cystitis (painful bladder syndrome). The usual dose is 100 mg three times daily taken on an empty stomach; symptomatic benefit may take several weeks to months. Although its exact mechanism is unknown, it is thought to adhere to the bladder wall mucosa and help restore the deficient protective glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide) layer, reducing irritant penetration and pain. Because it has weak anticoagulant and fibrinolytic activity (about 1/15 that of heparin), it can increase bleeding risk, especially with other anticoagulants/antiplatelets or in patients with bleeding risk factors. A notable long-term safety concern is pigmentary maculopathy (a retinal pigmentary disorder) reported with prolonged use - patients should have baseline and periodic eye examinations and report vision changes. It is contraindicated in patients hypersensitive to the drug or structurally related compounds.
indications: Relief of bladder pain or discomfort associated with interstitial cystitis (painful bladder syndrome)

dosage.n: Take with water 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals; reassess at ~3 months

dosage.d: Continue 100 mg three times daily; reassess benefit at 6 months if no improvement by 3 months
dosage.n: Discontinue if no benefit after adequate trial; monitor for maculopathy on long-term use

admin: Take orally with water at least 1 hour before meals or 2 hours after meals (empty stomach)
Swallow capsules whole; symptomatic relief may take 4 weeks to several months
Obtain a baseline retinal (ophthalmologic) examination and repeat periodically, particularly with long-term use
Assess bleeding risk and review concurrent anticoagulant/antiplatelet/NSAID use before starting
Reassess the need for ongoing therapy if there is no clinical benefit after an adequate trial
moa: The precise mechanism of action of pentosan polysulfate sodium in interstitial cystitis is not known. It is a low-molecular-weight, semisynthetic heparinoid (sulfated polysaccharide) that is thought to adhere to the bladder wall urothelium, where it may act as a buffer or protective coating, supplementing or restoring the deficient glycosaminoglycan (mucopolysaccharide) layer that normally shields the bladder mucosa from irritating solutes in urine. By reinforcing this protective layer, it is believed to reduce irritant penetration and the associated bladder pain. The drug also possesses weak anticoagulant and fibrinolytic (heparin-like) activity.

absolute: Known hypersensitivity to pentosan polysulfate sodium, structurally related compounds, or excipients
relative: Active bleeding or bleeding disorders / increased bleeding risk
Concurrent anticoagulant, antiplatelet, or high-dose NSAID therapy
Recent surgery, aneurysm, thrombocytopenia, hemophilia, gastrointestinal ulceration/polyps/diverticula
monitor: Visual symptoms / retinal pigmentary maculopathy (baseline and periodic eye exams)
Signs of bleeding (rectal hemorrhage, bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding)

preg: There are limited data on use in pregnancy. Because it is a heparin-like compound with anticoagulant activity, it should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed and the potential benefit justifies the potential risk. Discuss bleeding considerations with the obstetric team.
lact: It is not known whether pentosan polysulfate sodium is excreted in human milk. Data are limited; use caution and weigh the benefits of breastfeeding against the potential risk to the infant.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is established for renal impairment; use with caution and monitor for adverse effects, including bleeding.
hepatic: Use with caution in patients with hepatic impairment, since the weak anticoagulant/fibrinolytic activity may increase bleeding risk in patients with compromised liver function. Monitor liver function and for bleeding.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin, heparin, direct oral anticoagulants) - additive bleeding risk
Antiplatelet agents (aspirin, clopidogrel) - increased bleeding risk
moderate: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) - additive bleeding/GI risk
minor: Other drugs affecting platelet function or coagulation may add to bleeding tendency
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach (1 hour before or 2 hours after food) for optimal absorption.
interactions.alcohol: Limit alcohol - may add to gastrointestinal irritation and bleeding risk.
interactions.diagnostics: Baseline and periodic retinal examination for pigmentary maculopathy; monitor for bleeding and liver function where indicated.

serious: Pigmentary maculopathy / retinal pigmentary disorder (with long-term use), with potential vision impairment

monitoring: Baseline ophthalmologic (retinal) examination and periodic monitoring, especially with cumulative long-term use, for pigmentary maculopathy
Signs and symptoms of bleeding, particularly with concurrent anticoagulants/antiplatelets/NSAIDs
Liver function in patients with hepatic risk factors
Reassess clinical benefit at ~3-6 months and discontinue if ineffective
counsel: This medicine helps protect the bladder lining to relieve interstitial cystitis pain; it can take several weeks to a few months to work
Take it on an empty stomach with water, at least 1 hour before or 2 hours after eating
Have regular eye exams and report any vision changes (blurriness, trouble reading, difficulty adjusting to dim light) - long-term use has been linked to a retinal problem
Tell your doctor about any bleeding (rectal bleeding, easy bruising, nosebleeds) and inform providers before surgery; this drug has a mild blood-thinning effect
Some hair thinning can occur and usually reverses after stopping; report severe stomach pain or persistent diarrhea
pk: Symptomatic relief typically gradual, over weeks to months (often 4 weeks or longer)
Low oral bioavailability (~3% of the active drug is absorbed)
Reported elimination half-life of absorbed drug roughly 24-27 hours (with tissue affinity for uroepithelium)
Dosed three times daily; clinical benefit reassessed over months
Store at controlled room temperature, protected from moisture; keep out of reach of children
pearls: Mechanism is incompletely understood - thought to coat the bladder and restore the protective glycosaminoglycan layer; symptom relief is slow (weeks to months)
Long-term use is associated with PIGMENTARY MACULOPATHY (a retinal pigment disorder) - perform baseline and periodic retinal exams and counsel patients to report vision changes
Heparin-like weak anticoagulant/fibrinolytic activity (~1/15 of heparin) increases bleeding risk - caution with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, NSAIDs, and around surgery
Take on an empty stomach; absorption is low (~3%)
Reversible alopecia is a characteristic adverse effect
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered (ideally still on an empty stomach). If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the usual three-times-daily schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: There is limited experience with overdose. Anticipated effects relate to the drug's pharmacology, chiefly bleeding (consistent with its anticoagulant/fibrinolytic activity) and gastrointestinal disturbance. There is no specific antidote. In case of significant overdose, monitor for and manage bleeding with supportive care and appropriate hematologic measures, and provide symptomatic treatment for gastrointestinal effects.
